Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC)

Source: R/ancombc.r
ancombc.Rd

Estimates each feature's log fold change for every covariate of a linear model, corrected for the bias that differing sampling fractions cause, with standard errors and p-values (Lin & Peddada 2020, 2024). ancombc() is ANCOM-BC; ancombc2() is ANCOM-BC2, which also corrects each sample's logs for its estimated sampling fraction before refitting, adds a variance floor for rare features, uses t tests, and by default treats zeros as missing values instead of adding a pseudocount. Both follow scikit-bio's ancombc() and ancombc2().

Usage

ancombc(
  counts,
  formula,
  data,
  groups = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  pseudocount = NULL,
  max_iters = 100L,
  tol = 1e-05,
  alpha = 0.05,
  p_adjust = "holm",
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

ancombc2(
  counts,
  formula,
  data,
  groups = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  pseudocount = 0,
  var_quantile = 0.05,
  max_iters = 100L,
  tol = 1e-05,
  alpha = 0.05,
  p_adjust = "holm",
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of non-negative abundances (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the objects listed under Input Types. Counts, proportions, and the output of replace_zeros() are all accepted: each sample's scale is absorbed by its sampling fraction.

formula

The model, a one-sided formula over the columns of data, such as ~ status + age, or the same as a string ('status + age', with or without the ~). Anything stats::model.matrix() accepts may be used, including interactions (status * age) and a model without an intercept (~ 0 + status). Every factor is coded with treatment contrasts (see Covariates).

data

A data frame of sample metadata, with the variables of formula. Its rows are matched to the samples of counts by name when both have names (rows for other samples are left out), else by position. A single vector or factor is taken as one variable named group.

groups

NULL (the default), or the name of a categorical variable of data that is a term of formula, with at least three levels: the grouping the post-hoc tests (ancombc_global(), ancombc_pairwise(), ancombc_dunnett(), ancombc_trend()) compare by default. It doesn't change the results (scikit-bio's grouping).

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

pseudocount

The value added to every abundance before taking logs. For ancombc(), NULL (the default) follows the shared rule: nothing is added when counts has no zeros, else half the smallest non-zero value, with a warning. For ancombc2(), the default 0 adds nothing and treats zeros as missing values, as scikit-bio and ANCOMBC do; a positive value is added to every value instead.

max_iters

The most iterations of the bias-estimating EM algorithm, per covariate. Default: 100.

tol

The EM's convergence tolerance, on the Euclidean norm of the change in its eight parameters. Default: 1e-5.

alpha

The significance level of the adjusted p-values: reject is p_adjusted <= alpha. Strictly between 0 and 1. Default: 0.05.

p_adjust

How to adjust the p-values for multiple testing, over the features, separately for each covariate: any method of stats::p.adjust() ('holm', the default, 'hochberg', 'hommel', 'bonferroni', 'BH', 'BY', 'fdr', 'none').

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

var_quantile

ancombc2() only: the quantile of each covariate's coefficient variances (over the features) added to every variance of that covariate, which keeps rare features with tiny standard errors from looking significant (ANCOMBC's s0_perc). Between 0 and 1; 0 turns it off. Default: 0.05.

Value

A data frame of class c('ecodive_ancombc', 'data.frame'), one row per feature and covariate (the covariates of the first feature, then those of the second, and so on), with columns:

  • feature: the feature's name (its index, as text, when counts has no feature names).

  • covariate: the column of the design, as stats::model.matrix() names it: (Intercept), statusmoderate, age, statusmoderate:age, ... (scikit-bio's Intercept, status[T.moderate], ...).

  • log_fc: the bias-corrected coefficient, a natural-log fold change (scikit-bio's Log(FC)).

  • se: its standard error.

  • w: the test statistic, log_fc / se.

  • p_value: two-sided, from the standard normal (ancombc()) or a t distribution (ancombc2()).

  • p_adjusted: p_value adjusted with p_adjust, within each covariate.

  • reject: TRUE when p_adjusted <= alpha.

A coefficient that can't be estimated (with zeros as missing values, a feature whose observed samples leave a factor with fewer than two levels, or no samples at all) has NaN for log_fc, se and w, a p_value of 1 (which counts in the adjustment) and reject = FALSE, as in scikit-bio and ANCOMBC.

Attributes:

  • method: 'ancombc' or 'ancombc2'.

  • formula, groups, alpha, p_adjust, max_iters, tol, pseudocount (the value used), and for ancombc2() var_quantile.

  • The fit, for the post-hoc tests: coef (features \(\times\) covariates: the bias-corrected coefficients, including those that can't be estimated), var (their variances; for ancombc2() adjusted for the bias's uncertainty and var_quantile), vcov (features \(\times\) covariates \(\times\) covariates: each feature's covariance matrix, with var on its diagonal), dof (NULL for ancombc(); each feature's residual degrees of freedom for ancombc2()), estimable (NULL when every coefficient could be estimated, else a logical features \(\times\) covariates matrix), and design (the samples \(\times\) covariates model matrix, with stats::model.matrix()'s assign and contrasts attributes, the formula's term.labels, and xlevels, the levels of each factor).

  • bias: covariates \(\times\) 3, each covariate's estimated bias (delta_em, subtracted from the coefficients), its weighted least squares estimate (delta_wls) and that estimate's variance (var_delta); n_iters: the EM iterations run per covariate.

  • sample_fractions (ancombc2()): each sample's estimated log sampling fraction.

Details

The sampling fraction. A sample's sequencing reads are an unknown fraction of its community's absolute abundance, and that fraction differs from sample to sample. In the log scale it shifts every feature of a sample equally, so a naive log fold change between groups is off by the groups' difference in mean log sampling fraction, the same for every feature: ANCOM-BC estimates that shift (the bias) from the distribution of all features' coefficients and removes it.

With \(L\) the \(n \times D\) table of logs (natural logs of the abundance plus pseudocount) and \(X\) the design:

  1. Each feature's coefficients are fitted by least squares, \(\hat\beta_f = X^+ L_f\), and each sample's mean residual over the features estimates its log sampling fraction. Each coefficient's variance is a sandwich estimate from the residuals around those.

  2. For each covariate, an EM algorithm fits a three-part normal mixture to the features' coefficients: null features, centred on the bias \(\delta\), and features that decrease or increase. The bias is subtracted from that covariate's coefficients.

  3. ancombc() tests \(W = \hat\beta / \mathrm{se}\) against the standard normal.

ancombc2() centres each feature's logs first; after step 2 it estimates every sample's sampling fraction, subtracts it from the sample's logs, and fits again (now without sample effects); it then widens each variance to \((\mathrm{se} + \sqrt{\mathrm{var}_\delta})^2\), for the bias's uncertainty, adds the var_quantile quantile of the covariate's variances, and tests against a t distribution with each feature's residual degrees of freedom (observed samples minus the rank of its design). With zeros as missing values, each feature is fitted on its observed samples, the sample effects and coefficients being refined in turn (up to 20 rounds, to a tolerance of 0.01), as in ANCOMBC. Because that fit stops early, rescaling some samples' abundances moves the results a little (by up to about 0.1 in log_fc in a test with 30 samples), as it does in scikit-bio and ANCOMBC; without missing values, any per-sample scaling is absorbed exactly.

The EM stops after max_iters iterations even if it hasn't converged (attr(, 'n_iters') shows how many ran). Its estimate then depends on the exact path of its minimisations, so it can differ from ANCOMBC's by much more than when it converges (by 0.02 in one test).

Covariates

Character and logical variables become factors; every factor is coded with treatment contrasts, even an ordered one, and its unused levels are dropped. The reference level is a factor's first level, or for character variables the first value in sorted order (sort(method = 'radix'), C-locale order, as scikit-bio's), so that the results match scikit-bio's. To choose the reference, make the variable a factor with that level first, e.g. with stats::relevel(). A numeric variable is one covariate, its slope.

With zeros as missing values (ancombc2()), a feature that is missing from every sample of a factor's reference level is fitted against its first observed level instead, and the coefficients re-expressed, as ANCOMBC does (not for factors in an interaction). A feature whose observed samples leave a factor with fewer than two levels can't be estimated (see Value).

Differences from scikit-bio and ANCOMBC

The results are those of scikit-bio's ancombc() and ancombc2() (0.7.4), whose algorithm is followed step by step, including its reproduction of ANCOMBC's handling of zeros, failed fits and missing reference levels. The EM's one-dimensional minimisations use SciPy's Nelder-Mead rules, as scikit-bio does; ANCOMBC uses nloptr's, so its estimates differ slightly, by about 1e-5, when the EM converges. Also, unlike ANCOMBC:

  • var_quantile = 0 adds nothing, as in scikit-bio; ANCOMBC's s0_perc = 0 adds the smallest variance.

  • The pseudoinverse is of the design itself, with numpy's cutoff; ANCOMBC inverts \(X'X\) with MASS::ginv(), whose tolerance drops columns of a badly scaled design (e.g. a covariate in the tens of thousands), and then gives wrong standard errors.

  • With zeros as missing values, a factor in an interaction is not re-expressed against a feature-local reference level (scikit-bio's choice), so such features' coefficients differ from ANCOMBC's.

And unlike both:

  • The covariates are named as stats::model.matrix() names them, and ordered as in R (patsy puts categorical terms before numeric ones).

  • Zeros in ancombc(): scikit-bio refuses them; ecodive applies its shared pseudocount rule (see pseudocount).

  • Not carried over: random effects (ANCOMBC's rand_formula), scikit-bio's aggregator, ANCOMBC's data preprocessing (prv_cut, lib_cut, tax_level; see the examples), its structural-zero detection and its pseudocount sensitivity analysis (repeat the call with other pseudocount values).

  • A design with as many columns as samples, or more, is an error (the residuals would all be zero); a rank-deficient design gives a warning.

  • The p-values of each covariate are adjusted with stats::p.adjust() over the features whose p-value isn't NaN, as scikit-bio does.

Computation. The per-feature fits and variances run in parallel C, over blocks of features, and the EM in parallel over covariates. Results are identical for any number of cpus, and for dense and sparse counts. Memory: the \(n \times D\) table of logs, plus \(P^2\) doubles per feature for the covariances (and, with zeros as missing, each feature's masked-design decomposition).

Same names in other packages

ANCOMBC (Bioconductor) has ancombc() and ancombc2(), the original implementations, which take a phyloseq or TreeSummarizedExperiment object and preprocess it; scikit-bio (Python) has the functions this follows.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

References

Lin, H., & Peddada, S. D. (2020). Analysis of compositions of microbiomes with bias correction. Nature Communications, 11, 3514.

Lin, H., & Peddada, S. D. (2024). Multigroup analysis of compositions of microbiomes with covariate adjustments and repeated measures. Nature Methods, 21, 83–91.

See also

ancom(), dirmult_ttest(), replace_zeros().

Examples

    # scikit-bio's example: three disease states and age.
    x <- rbind(
      c(2, 0, 7, 0, 0, 2, 3, 2), c(0, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 0),
      c(3, 1, 0, 9, 0, 1, 1, 0), c(2, 0, 1, 8, 1, 0, 11, 46),
      c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2), c(0, 3, 22, 1, 1, 1, 3, 0),
      c(1, 7, 16, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2), c(0, 5, 6, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1),
      c(1, 7, 0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2), c(0, 6, 4, 2, 0, 2, 2, 1),
      c(3, 13, 7, 0, 0, 0, 3, 9), c(1, 8, 5, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
      c(0, 5, 14, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1), c(5, 26, 3, 2, 0, 3, 1, 3),
      c(0, 18, 7, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0) )
    dimnames(x) <- list(paste0('S', 1:15), paste0('F', 1:8))
    meta <- data.frame(
      status = rep(c('mild', 'moderate', 'severe'), each = 5),
      age    = c(39, 19, 20, 31, 15, 37, 27, 47, 26, 23, 39, 48, 46, 33, 36),
      row.names = rownames(x) )

    res <- ancombc(x + 1, ~ status + age, meta)
    res[res$reject & res$covariate != '(Intercept)', ]
#>    feature      covariate     log_fc        se        w      p_value
#> 6       F2 statusmoderate 1.90555337 0.2585194 7.371028 1.693178e-13
#> 7       F2   statussevere 2.93516110 0.3041880 9.649167 4.955686e-22
#> 12      F3            age 0.06264515 0.0218213 2.870825 4.094016e-03
#>      p_adjusted reject
#> 6  1.354542e-12   TRUE
#> 7  3.964549e-21   TRUE
#> 12 3.275213e-02   TRUE

    # ANCOM-BC2, with zeros as missing values.
    res2 <- ancombc2(x, ~ status + age, meta, groups = 'status')
    head(res2)
#>   feature      covariate      log_fc         se          w    p_value
#> 1      F1    (Intercept)  0.47551804 1.43509935  0.3313485 0.75381787
#> 2      F1 statusmoderate -0.29466034 1.04951557 -0.2807584 0.79014246
#> 3      F1   statussevere  0.85379160 1.57309664  0.5427458 0.61061281
#> 4      F1            age -0.03289532 0.06543709 -0.5027015 0.63652850
#> 5      F2    (Intercept) -1.44347145 1.28795186 -1.1207495 0.29490815
#> 6      F2 statusmoderate  1.96595194 0.91658832  2.1448582 0.06428813
#>   p_adjusted reject
#> 1   1.000000  FALSE
#> 2   1.000000  FALSE
#> 3   1.000000  FALSE
#> 4   1.000000  FALSE
#> 5   1.000000  FALSE
#> 6   0.514305  FALSE

    # ANCOMBC's preprocessing, done first: keep features present in at
    # least 10% of samples (prv_cut = 0.1), and samples with at least 10
    # reads (lib_cut = 10).
    x <- x[, colMeans(x > 0) >= 0.1, drop = FALSE]
    x <- x[rowSums(x) >= 10, , drop = FALSE]
